clue.text: Where one may spend time underground

definitions.text: Where one may spend time underground

parts.words: Where one may spend time underground
parts.note: doing time means serving a prison sentence, and the old castle cell lay below ground level

explanation.surface: Sounds like a question about a cave, a mine or a cellar where someone passes the hours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spend time' hints at serving a sentence rather than merely passing hours.
explanation.definitionFit: A castle's underground prison is where captives served their time, below the keep.

clue.text: Shade of grievance

definitions.meaning: shade or shadow, from the Latin umbra
a sense of offence, as in taking offence

explanation.surface: A shade of colour named after a complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: The word once meant shadow, and now means resentment, as in taking offence at something.

clue.text: Big jar, say

indicators.note: say tells us the word is spoken, so its sound gives the answer

parts.note: to jar is to grate, to irritate harshly

explanation.surface: Describing a large jar, as an example of something big.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jar' looks like a pot but is the verb, to grate on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Big and large are both sizes far above ordinary, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Having our nose put out of joint is hard to bear

indicators.note: put out of joint, like a dislocated limb, says these letters are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: Being offended, having one's nose put out of joint, is difficult to endure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put out of joint' rearranges OURNOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Onerous duties are burdensome, heavy and difficult to carry out, a dictionary synonym.

clue.text: Commercials about fitting suits

indicators.note: about says the word for adverts goes around the other piece

parts.note: commercials are adverts, shortened to ads
fitting means proper or deserved, which is just

explanation.surface: Adverts for tailoring that show how a suit fits the customer.
explanation.definitionFit: To suit something is to adapt or tailor it so it fits, a verb synonym in the third person.

clue.text: I decry the making of gas for stage effect

indicators.note: the making of says these letters are the raw material, to be shaped into something new

explanation.surface: A critic complaining about the smoke machine in a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the making of' rearranges IDECRY.
explanation.definitionFit: Frozen carbon dioxide gives off dense white vapour that creates the low mist seen on stage.

clue.text: A theatregoer's guide

parts.note: a guide is read as a person who shows the audience to their seats, not a handbook

explanation.surface: Looks like a handbook listing shows to see.
explanation.walkthrough: 'guide' suggests a book or listings magazine, but it is the woman who leads people to their seats.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman employed in a theatre or cinema to show patrons to their seats has this job title.

clue.text: He made an unexceptional plea for blessing

definitions.text: He made an unexceptional plea for blessing

parts.words: He made an unexceptional plea for blessing
parts.note: unexceptional is read as excepting nobody: the boy in Dickens's A Christmas Carol says God bless us, every one

explanation.surface: Someone said an ordinary, unremarkable prayer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unexceptional' looks like dull, but means making no exceptions: 'every one'.
explanation.definitionFit: The frail Cratchit boy of A Christmas Carol famously asks God to bless us, every one.

clue.text: Get back to front

parts.note: read not as reversing something but as returning to first place in a race

explanation.walkthrough: 'back to front' looks like the idiom for something reversed; here it is getting back to the front of the field.
explanation.definitionFit: A competitor who retakes first place after being overtaken returns to the head of the race.

clue.text: The Spanish scholar returned, qualified

indicators.note: returned says the Spanish article and the degree are read backwards together

parts.note: el is Spanish for the
BA, Bachelor of Arts, stands for a scholar

explanation.surface: A Spanish academic has come home with the qualifications he went abroad for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns ELBA round as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone qualified has the skill or competence needed, so is capable of doing the job.

clue.text: Extremely slender, for example, that's about all

indicators.note: about says the abbreviation for example wraps around the other words

parts.note: for example is abbreviated eg
extremely means very
slender means thin

explanation.surface: A description of someone very thin, offered as the last word on the matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts VERYTHIN inside EG, so E opens and G closes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: All and the whole lot both mean the complete total of things, a plain synonym.

clue.text: He is part of America's troubles

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A man described as being a contributor to the problems of the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is close to &lit: Fidel, Cuba's leader, was long one of America's troubles. 'He' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Fidel the Cuban revolutionary leader is a man, so the pronoun stands for him in this clue.

clue.text: Account by clergyman should be reliable

parts.note: a curate is an assistant parish priest, a clergyman

explanation.surface: A vicar's report ought to be trustworthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Something reliable is correct and trustworthy, close in sense to precise and exact.

clue.text: Play the part of engineer on stage

parts.note: RE stands for the Royal Engineers, the British Army's engineering corps
to present a show is to put it on stage

explanation.surface: An engineer taking a role in an amateur play.
explanation.definitionFit: To act as a character is to portray or stand in for them, a synonym phrase.

clue.text: Ringleader felt urge to reform, being contrite

parts.note: the leader, or first letter, of ring is R

indicators.note: to reform says the letters are formed again in another order

explanation.surface: A gang's leader felt an urge to go straight, showing remorse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ringleader' is read as the leading letter of ring; 'to reform' rearranges FELTURGE into EGRETFUL.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone contrite is sorry and remorseful, wishing a deed undone.

clue.text: Put one's foot down, as a matter of duty

definitions.meaning: to bring a foot down hard on the ground
... duty is a British tax paid on property purchases and documents

explanation.surface: Someone being firm and insisting, as is their obligation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put one's foot down' looks like the idiom for being firm, but it is meant literally. Stamp duty is a UK tax on buying property.
explanation.definitionFit: Stamping is bringing the foot down heavily; a duty stamp is the mark showing tax was paid.

clue.text: Their victims got it in the neck

definitions.text: Their victims got it in the neck

parts.words: Their victims got it in the neck
parts.note: the idiom for being punished is taken literally, recalling the historical Indian robber gangs whose method targeted the throat

explanation.surface: People on the receiving end of a scolding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got it in the neck' is the idiom for being severely told off; here it is taken literally, after the historical Thuggee gangs of India.
explanation.definitionFit: The word comes from the Thuggee robber gangs of India and now means violent criminals in general.

clue.text: Unusual hoarder of fish eggs

indicators.note: unusual says the letters of the word hoarder appear in an uncommon order

explanation.surface: An odd collector who stockpiles caviar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' rearranges HOARDER.
explanation.definitionFit: The firm mass of eggs in a female fish is distinguished from the soft milt of the male.

clue.text: Yet civilians lived such a life in the war

definitions.text: Yet civilians lived such a life in the war

parts.words: Yet civilians lived such a life in the war
parts.note: a protected life usually means a cosy one, yet civilians in wartime literally spent nights in air-raid refuges

explanation.surface: A paradox about wartime: ordinary people had it easy, yet endured bombing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'such a life' brings to mind the phrase for a protected, unworldly upbringing, the opposite of wartime hardship; the 'Yet' points at the irony.
explanation.definitionFit: During air raids civilians took refuge in bomb shelters, so they literally lived protected lives.

clue.text: Many snakes are associated with them

definitions.text: Many snakes are associated with them

parts.words: Many snakes are associated with them
parts.note: points to the children's board game Snakes and ..., where the two climb and slide side by side

explanation.surface: A natural history remark about which creatures live near snakes.
explanation.walkthrough: The snakes are those on a game board, not reptiles.
explanation.definitionFit: In the board game, players climb these and slide down snakes, so the two are always paired.

clue.text: When there's a change of plea, men select a jury

indicators.note: change of says the letters of the following words are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: In court, a defendant alters their plea and men are chosen as jurors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change of' rearranges PLEA and MEN together.
explanation.definitionFit: To impanel is to enrol the twelve jurors for a trial, choosing them from a list.

clue.text: Abandon school subject and make one's name as a writer

parts.note: RE is religious education, a subject taught in British schools

parts.words: make one's name as a writer
parts.note: to write one's name on a document is to sign it

explanation.surface: Someone quits teaching to win fame as an author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make one's name' looks like becoming famous, but it is writing your signature.
explanation.definitionFit: To abandon a post is to quit it, giving it up formally.

clue.text: A gastronomic treat?

parts.note: treat is read as paying for someone, so the dinner costs the diner nothing

explanation.surface: A description of a delicious, special dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treat' suggests something delightful to eat, but it is the sense of someone else paying the bill.
explanation.definitionFit: When another person treats you, you eat without paying, so dinner comes at no charge.

clue.text: Put new pep into endless diet with port

indicators.note: into says the reworked letters go inside the shortened word
endless says the word diet loses its final letter
new says the letters of pep are formed afresh in another order

explanation.surface: Advice to liven up a dull diet with a glass of port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' makes EPP from pep; 'endless' cuts diet to DIE; 'into' puts EPP inside DIE.
explanation.definitionFit: Dieppe is a ferry and fishing harbour on the Normandy coast of France, an example of a port.

clue.text: Huge cost of electrical safety precaution

definitions.meaning: something very expensive is said to cost the world, a British idiom
a wire connecting an appliance to the ground so a fault current drains away safely

explanation.surface: Wiring a building safely turns out to be very expensive.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage a ground wire is called by this name, and 'it costs the ...' is an idiom for very expensive.
explanation.definitionFit: Paying the planet is the idiom for great expense; in Britain the ground connection on a plug has this name.

clue.text: Pet of a girl, perhaps, but recklessly extravagant

indicators.note: perhaps says these letters are one possible arrangement, here to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A girl's darling who turns out to be a wild spendthrift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges PETOFAGIRL.
explanation.definitionFit: A profligate person wastes money freely, spending far beyond sense, a dictionary synonym.

clue.text: Small pig has nose tip stuck in furrow

indicators.note: stuck in says that letter is pushed inside the groove

parts.note: a rut is a furrow or groove in the ground

indicators.note: tip says only the leading letter of the word nose is used

explanation.surface: A little piglet rooting about with its snout in a ploughed field.
explanation.definitionFit: The weakest, smallest piglet of a litter is called by this name, a farming term.

clue.text: Sense and Sensibility?

definitions.meaning: a sense such as touch, or a hunch or intuition
sensibility is emotional responsiveness, the capacity for emotion

explanation.surface: The title of Jane Austen's novel, Sense and Sensibility.
explanation.walkthrough: The book title has to be split: each half is a separate definition, and 'and' joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: Touch is one sense, and emotional responsiveness is sensibility; the word covers both.

clue.text: Used when a path's relaid around lake?

definitions.text: Used when a path's relaid around lake?

indicators.note: around says the reworked letters go round the abbreviation
relaid says the letters are laid down again in a different order

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for lake on maps

explanation.surface: A question about what material is used to resurface a footpath beside a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'relaid' rearranges A PATHS (the 's counts as an S) and 'around' puts that round L. The whole clue describes the material.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarmac-like bitumen surfacing is what is laid down when paths and roads are resurfaced.
